verdict: OK to lend in Bengaluru defence and aerospace parts — pursue Nadcap-qualified precision machinists with real Safran/Tier-1 contracts; avoid pre-revenue startups and single-customer shops.
title: Bengaluru defence & aerospace parts: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**These are precision machining and special-process shops — turning, milling, surface and heat treatment — that convert certified raw material into flight-approved parts for global primes and Indian defence programmes.** Cash comes from a qualified part number: once a customer approves your process, the part is sole-sourced for years and pricing holds. Value sits in the qualification (Nadcap approvals, customer audits), not in the machines. So when a proposal lands, check the Nadcap and customer-approval list first; if the shop has no approved special processes, ask what stops the next shop from taking the order. JJG Aero's third plant is INR 200 crore on 12 acres, with phase one at 325,000 sqft against roughly 100,000 sqft across two existing plants [3]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the capex is matched by a signed order book; if the borrower is building ahead of contracts, ask for the customer letter of intent. ## What has changed now
**The cycle is genuinely strong.** India-wide IIP for NIC 30 output is +25.3% YoY and +22.7% Apr-to-date [D]. Karnataka GST collections are +11.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, and electricity demand +23.3% against +9.5% [D]. Locally, JJG Aero broke ground on its third plant on 19 October 2026 and won new Safran Landing Systems contracts, expanding from one Safran division to three [3]. Peer results agree: Raymond's aerospace revenue rose 72% to ₹139 crore at a 21% operating margin [4]; Goodluck Defence revenue +31%, EBITDA +46%, PAT +67% [7]. Note the local news is thin — one startup funding round [1][2] and one plant groundbreaking [3] — so lean on first principles and peers for the rest. ## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue established Tier-2 machinists with multi-division prime relationships and in-house special processes; avoid pre-revenue startups and single-customer shops.** Venttup raised $3 million and plans a Bengaluru factory, but its case study names no customer and does not establish flight use [1] — that is equity risk, not bank risk. Client concentration is the real killer: Paras Defence's top three clients were 71% of order book and top five 63% of FY2021 revenue [9]. So structure term loans against the plant with a DSRA, and working capital against certified receivables only. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch the gap between order book and billing, and the Q4 concentration.** Defence billing clusters with more than 70% of sales in Q4, inflating working capital at year-end [11]. If a borrower's top client crosses 50% of revenue, ask for a second qualified customer before enhancing limits.
watch: Top client above 50% of revenue -> freeze limit enhancement until a second qualified customer is added
Billed vs unbilled and Q4 billing share (quarterly)
Q4 share above 70% of annual sales [11] -> require higher DSRA before term-loan disbursal
Any approval lapsed or withdrawn -> treat as a default event and review the facility
